column2: And this. Someone near the ration station asked me to bring it for a valuation. Don't buy it yet. Appraise it. I want to hear what you'd quote too.
Tool awaiting appraisal
You've already written that one up. Don't do it twice just to hear another compliment.
That's enough appraising for now. While you were looking at it, something else came to mind.
The locket needs a 2×2 space. Existing items are preserved; move it into room and its shape will be updated.
Each item is priced separately. Bargain or pass; we can still talk.
Leave the order. I'll see what I can prepare.
That's the business noted. There's something just for you, too.
That's the budget spent. Everything collected is paid for. I'll find another way to source the rest.
Here for the tools-and-materials order. I've collected {0} tools and {1} materials; {2} credits remain. Show me what you have. We settle each purchase as we go.
I'll pass this time. Don't let me hold up your search.
That's everything. Goods collected, accounts settled. Don't look so surprised. I really did come to give you some business.
The tools-and-materials order has closed. Delivered goods were paid for; the remaining supplies will be sourced elsewhere.
Mother asked me to bring a small request too. Decide whether you want it. Don't say yes just because I brought it.

Two working tools and one ordinary material item. Six hundred in buying funds; we'll inspect and price the goods together. I'll come in two days. If you're short then, you've another four days. Don't empty your own shelves for it.
I'll take these. I'll ask about the rest in two days. Don't buy bad goods just to finish the order.
Interested in the order?

2 tool items and 1 material item. Total buying funds: 600; prices negotiated and paid on delivery. Due four days after the first collection visit. Declining or missing it does not change the relationship or rescue.
Proper business today. They need tools, materials and household goods upstairs. I'm buying for them, with nine hundred to spend. Goods first. I'll tell you about the launch afterwards.
I'm bringing something for a valuation today. Relax. They want to know what the item is worth, not how much your young lady has spent.
Some people near the ration station pooled money for tools and household goods. Quote normally. Don't give up your margin just because it's me.
All right, that's enough for today. The shop keeps opening; I keep getting on with life. We can deal with Wilde when we're ready.
Two items. My own goods; separate payment. Look them over. I promise the labels survived this time.
Keep it safe. And don't put that one on today's bill.
A sample from Eleanor's first order. Tip, grip and provenance checked. Already covered by the preparations; no further charge.
I'll keep the sample for you. Not taking stock doesn't stop me delivering my own order.
You haven't taken that sample yet. Room on the counter today? It's free. Don't start bargaining with me again.
Let's see the materials.
No stock this time. Tell me about upstairs.
I asked about two small lots on the way: tools or materials. Didn't commit you to either. Want a look? The pass and clothes are paid for. These goods are a separate purchase.
Which lot this time?
The lot you chose is still here. Don't rush. It hasn't grown legs.
Show me the tools.
Here. Look them over. We can take our time with the price.
Take the crate and put it on the counter.
You can inspect it later, or hand it to her directly.
Accept it.
She has started noticing what you need.
Take it, but inspect the crate first.
The stolen-goods record will show up. It may also draw attention.
I'll take them. It's compensation for the negotiation.
Taking the money doesn't mean you've priced her mother.
Give it to you and your mother for living costs.
You don't keep the money; it should go to the people who need it.
I won't take it.
You don't want this to look like a sale.
I care about you. But not that way.
Friends route; the rescue is not undone.
I want to know you better. Can we take it slower?
No affection penalty; one more confirmation later.
I like you too. It has nothing to do with where you used to live.
Accept her feelings clearly.
You keep it. It is safer with you.
She holds the drive; you cannot sell it behind her back.
This is too much. I can't be involved anymore.
The line ends here. She will not trust you with anything important again.
Leave it with me. No one takes it without asking you first.
You become the custodian; only you can hand it over.
I want you to come here as more than a regular.
Confirm the 'slower' answer from before.
I've thought it through. Let's stay friends.
Choose friendship, ending the deferred romance decision.
Take the pheromone perfume.
An upper-district item. It might fetch a good price down here.
Take the portable water purifier.
She insists on thanking you. This one will last a while.
Do not mention the crate yet.
She will not know the danger; the trap remains armed.
Keep it. You need it more.
She still has an investigator to pay. Remember the thought.
Pay the normal price.
You do not want her gift to become another debt.
Use the slower ordinary review (cost {0} credits)
Requires a record from successfully exposing the fake uncle.
If it cannot be done, switch to the exchange.
Do not posture. Keep her mother alive first.
Use a Security review and temporary custody (Security rep {0}+, cost {1} credits)
Requires an existing frame-up or threat record.
Ask the upper district for named sponsorship (Upper District rep {0}+, cost {1} credits)
Trade the work log for acceptance. This is not buying a verdict.
Refuse and let him take it away.
If she never receives it, the trap cannot spring.
Keep it and sell it.
She is still saving for the investigator.
It looks better on you. I'll take the thought.
The locket stays with her.
Go back and raise the money. Return tomorrow.
She is still inside. You are not done trying.
Bring your mother back first. Return the research.
An exchange. Mother and daughter can reunite below, but the research is not published.
Secure the transfer and protection first. Decide who receives the research after she is safe.
Requires admissible material and a channel that actually responds.
Publish the research now.
She takes part in the decision, but no one can promise her mother will live.
This is too much. I'm stepping away.
A normal exit; she handles the rest herself.
Let her finish the investigation herself.
She earned the money. The decision is hers too.
Offer money in exchange for control (cost {0} credits)
She will refuse. Some things are not debts.
Give the drive to a newspaper without telling her.
You decide for her. This is not shared responsibility.
Then I'll keep it.
Accept her gift.
Tell her about the crate.
Let her know it was reported stolen, and not to touch it.
Hand him the drive and take the three hundred (+{0})
You decide what her mother is worth without her. The relationship ends.
Just make him leave.
Remember the offer and tell her next time. The threat remains.
Hand the record to Security (Security rep {0}+)
Requires an existing frame-up or threat record, and a channel that actually responds.
Sell the drive to a black-market buyer (+{0})
They promise nothing about her mother. The research leaves both your hands.
Ask the upper district to make contact (Upper District rep {0}+)
Trade the research work log for a verifiable response.

The continuing supply contracts are settled too. From tomorrow your share is 600 credits a day. The earlier accounts still stand. Don't call it paying back my wages. This is business we built together.

Once the first order is settled, a share goes to you. From tomorrow, I'll set aside 200 credits a day and bring it when I visit. Missing a visit won't lose you anything. Your capital and the goods we checked together are part of this business.
After the business opens, daily dividends rise to 600 credits, paid during visits.
After the first order succeeds, 200 credits accrue daily, paid during Eleanor's visits.
Here's your share: {0} credits. Everything set aside up to today. Count it. Don't look at me like that. My accounts aren't missing a line.
Keep it safe. I'll keep recording the rest and settle it next time I come.
Eleanor's dividend received: {0} credits. Still awaiting collection: {1}.
Dividends: {0}/day; awaiting collection {1}; received in total {2}.
Brought the accounts. Let's check these entries first. We can talk goods afterwards.
Eleanor's first visit moves from day 23 to day 12. The rest of her story schedule also moves 11 days earlier.
Old Echo
Put my name down. Let me get my coat.
Tomorrow evening. I'll pick you up.
Arrange the next party visit. Native important events take priority; no payment or outing is consumed.
Good. Tomorrow evening, then. Don't leave me waiting in the doorway.
I still can't leave. Go ahead without me.
She attends alone and won't ask again. Romance and dividends are unaffected.
Attend the party epilogue. No payment or evening outing is consumed.
Let's go. Today's time is yours.
She stands in the doorway in a fitted wine-red gown, bare shoulders catching the light, her earrings swaying gently. She waits for you to speak.
Back in her Upper Level clothes, her hair carefully arranged and earrings swaying gently, she waits in the doorway for you to speak.
Guest
Not tonight. I'll come to the next one.
After at least seven days, she'll ask once more during a suitable visit. Your relationship is unaffected.
Purchasing Manager

Eleanor, recently returned to the Upper Level through her own business, attended a party with a man seldom seen in society. Asked who he was, she introduced him as her partner, a pawnshop owner from the Lower Levels. Guests report that a purchasing manager who had sought a change in her business partners also approached to offer his greetings. The couple later took to the dance floor and left together.
Eleanor attends Upper Level party with mysterious companion
I still can't get away tomorrow.
She waits for your answer.
Decided? I'm waiting.
She puts away the notes she brought and lays down her pen, without reaching for her bag.
The clasp has been replaced. Fine old scratches remain on the band.
Lydia set it on the counter as if testing something.
Upper-District Handmade Bracelet
An old-fashioned locket with a nearly worn-away line on the back.
She pushed it across the counter, her fingers lingering on its edge.
Eleanor's Mother's Locket
Get something to eat for you and your roommate.
...She shared her portion with me yesterday.
The things I said before... I was wrong. I'm sorry.
Eat first. We can talk later.
...Don't go telling everyone about today.
(You put the three hundred credits into the till. Eleanor glances at it and says nothing.)
...I'll tell her you passed it on.
Are you sure? ...All right. I'll remember it.
(The goods Eleanor picked sell cleanly. She stands by the door and gives you a small, satisfied nod.)
(A little later, the customer Eleanor mentioned walks into the shop.)
The pawnshop stays open. She has work, her mother, and a pile of ordinary worries. She also has a reason to visit that no longer needs explaining.
This is for you. Don't ask the price.
(You leave this matter outside the door. She does not come back to ask, and does not explain.)
(You decide not to mention the crate yet.)
(She leaves the bottle of perfume on the counter. Only later do you realise it never runs empty.)
(She gets no food, and does not ask again. Before leaving, she folds the empty bag and puts it back in her pocket.)
When I have time, I'll come help you at the dump. We can search a few more piles together. I'll keep an eye out for any loose scrap.
(While she is not looking, you hand the drive to a newspaper. By the next morning the story is all over the station.)
(You sell the drive to someone else. They care only about the data, and never ask her mother's name.)
(You push the drive across. He picks it up and smiles politely. Three hundred credits arrive soon after.)
All right, agreed.
(The man claiming to be her uncle has not come back. The counter is clear.)
(You think for a moment, then decide to tell her about the man claiming to be her uncle.)
The later confirmed news is that her mother did not survive.
That will do for today. The goods decide whether a deal is right.
Eleanor said your stock was worth a look. Let's discuss the goods and price in person.
Keep it on you. If they come looking, they'll find me first — let them.
She keeps the drive on her person; you cannot sell it behind her back. Your shop takes the first knock.
Leave the drive with me. It's on my counter. No one takes it from there.
You become the custodian. Who receives it still needs her approval.
No additional payment. Continue with this choice.
I've decided. I'll leave the investigation, and our agreement ends here too.
Explicitly leave the investigation and end the attendant agreement. Return the drive and close future return projects. Paid support is delivered; no refund or reversal of existing rescue results.
I'll pass the message on. The door is that way.
Remember the offer and tell her next time. The threat remains.
Every word you said today will reach Security. (Security rep {0}+)
Requires an existing frame-up or threat record, and a channel that actually responds.
If you want to talk, have the Upper Level make a formal approach. (Upper Level rep {0}+)
Trade the research work log for a verifiable response.
Keep the drive with you. I'll tell you everything I knew then.
I will. Tell me what you knew, from the beginning.
You go through each thing that struck you as wrong. She listens, her hand resting on the papers.
Do the same from now on. Whoever holds the drive, I won't be kept in the dark.
Let me tell you the rest of that day. From now on, you see the records of everything I find.
Start with when you knew something was wrong. Don't just choose the parts you think won't upset me.
You tell her what happened from the beginning. She doesn't make it easier for you, but she doesn't put the papers away either.
I'll read them. Remember what you've promised.
I don't have a safer way right now. Let's lay out what we can do.
Tell me what you can't do. Don't comfort me with promises you can't keep.
We can negotiate the drive for her release. I have no firm answer on anything else.
Then let's start there. I understand what it means when you say you aren't sure.
Then come here. You don't need an errand as an excuse to see me.
...I'll still do the work. Don't take my place away the moment you say yes.
Your place stays yours. I love you too. Did you hear that?
I heard. Keep your voice down.
You hold out your hand. This time, she doesn't pretend to reach for the cloth.
I love you too. Stop using the counter as an excuse.
...Who says it was an excuse?
The same patch. Three times.
You counted, and still waited for me to say it first.
Then I won't wait now. Give me your hand.
Then come here. You don't need an errand as an excuse to see me.
Accept her confession and continue your attendant agreement.
You're important to me, but we should stay friends.
I love you too. End the agreement; let's just be lovers.
I love you too. Stop using the counter as an excuse.
I understand. Be my attendant, and my lover.
Confirm: publish now, before protection is secured.
Ends the attendant agreement and closes future return projects. Paid support is delivered, achievements remain, and resources are not refunded. Existing rescue results remain.
Looking for this pen?
How did you get it?
Retrieved it from where you put it. The wrong place. Second time now.
My attendant keeps a careful count.
If I don't, Master will spend all his searching time asking me.
That wouldn't be so bad.
...If you want to talk to me, say so. Don't use misplaced things as an excuse.
Brought something to eat. Don't ask what it cost first. I keep my own accounts.
Didn't you used to hate this sort of thing?
Still do. This place makes it edible, though.
Master only gets 'edible'?
It's the best portion I could find. Do you know how long I spent choosing?
Then I'll eat it properly.
Yes. Tell me afterward whether you'd like it again.
Someone at the door asked whether I worked here.
What did you say?
Yes. Then he asked whether I helped people like this upstairs too.
Did that annoy you?
A little. So I told him I only do this for Master. Anyone else couldn't hire me for any price.
I thought that name was private.
You're not allowed to use me to amuse people. Choosing to say it myself is different.
You're right.
Then stop smiling so much. ...At least wait until I turn around.
Looks quite tidy today. Nothing for me to do?
There is. Stay with me a while.
That counts?
Yes.
Then where do I sit?
Closer.
She sits beside you, her hand within reach. After a while, noticing that you're still reading the accounts, she brushes the back of your hand.
Master. You assigned the duty. Don't call someone over and then ignore her.
The reputation discount is active.
At Upper Level reputation ≥{0} and Lower Level reputation ≥{1}, the cost is halved: {2} → {3} credits. Reputation is not spent.
At Lower Level reputation ≥{0}, the cost is halved: {1} → {2} credits. Reputation is not spent.
You may pay the full price before meeting the reputation requirement.
At Upper Level reputation ≥{0}, the cost is halved: {1} → {2} credits. Reputation is not spent.
In time, people grow used to the Upper Level girl helping at the pawnshop. She remains particular with customers, and leaves no doubt when speaking up for the owner.
When someone offers more to hire her, she asks about the duties before the price. If they hope to buy that private name along with her work, she raises her chin and tells them to ask elsewhere.
The agreement hasn't expired. Neither of you is in a hurry. The pen beside the counter always points toward your usual hand.
Only when the shop holds just the two of you does she lean close and ask, 'Master, how long will you keep me waiting today?'
They have a place fit to live in. Enough light to read, and room at last for her mother's worktable.
She has passed through the Upper Level checkpoint again. Yet on her return, she still comes to your counter first.
She has begun signing business under her own name. Your preparations have become more than a word of thanks.
People upstairs have asked who you are. Every time, she calls you someone she trusts.
The Upper Level remembers her name. She intends to announce the agreement's fulfillment herself, and is still waiting for the right evening.

Later, when people upstairs mention Eleanor, they no longer speak only of the size of her mother's farm. They discuss her business, her eye for goods, and the person who still runs a pawnshop downstairs.

She never hides who supplied the first capital, or who prepared an opportunity before she had any. If someone thinks a higher offer would make her change masters, she asks them to distinguish business from fantasy.

After her own business, she still returns to you and changes into that outfit she has kept. You beckon, and the woman now earnestly invited throughout the Upper Level comes over with that familiar touch of pride.
'Shall I tell you about the world outside first, or simply stay with you a while, Master?'
Her mother's name returns upstairs too. Sometimes mother and daughter go up together, and come back together. Outside this pawnshop, her mother always pauses to straighten her daughter's collar.
Her mother keeps the notice overturning the conviction at the top of a drawer. Neither brings up the case anymore. Sometimes, at dinner, they simply set out an extra bowl.
The review documents have been submitted, but the formal notice has not arrived. She keeps every receipt safe, and after her own business, still goes home to eat with her mother.
First she checks your itinerary, then asks, item by item, what you're taking and leaving. You say there are no more duties. She ignores that until the last detail is settled.

Her mother's housing and her own future must follow the circumstances as they are. She doesn't pretend following you is as simple as saying it, but remembers how to contact you more carefully than you do.
At parting, she holds your hand. 'Master, tell me when you arrive. Don't always make me the last to know.'
She begins asking after you, checking every report that can be checked. When someone offers only a vague assurance, she asks who is responsible, and when she can see you.
Love doesn't automatically change the outcome. What she can do depends on how much room this ending leaves her.
But she remembers you telling her not to carry everything alone. Now it's her turn to verify the news, one piece at a time, and come find you.
She comes to the pawnshop once more. Standing at the counter, she almost asks what she should do first today.
No one answers. She puts the pen back beside your usual hand, stands for a long while, and finally leaves it untouched.
She still has to look after her mother, do business, and live. But there are ordinary instructions she will never hear again.
Sometimes she sends a short message. By the end, she always adds one question: are you still at that shop?
Once she writes that she saw a badly written price tag and almost rewrote it out of habit. The letter pauses there, then adds: remember to replace yours.

Later, you take no further part in the investigation. What needed returning is returned. The agreement and romantic progress end there. She must find her own way forward; you do not invent an ending that has not happened.
Let's leave it. Follow your own investigation plan.
Agreed. (Pay 800 credits)
You've arranged it. Go see the detective.
I can help with what comes next.

Opens the attendant romance and return upstairs. Cooperation starts with work; the private address develops later. Only final confirmation pays 800 in advance wages. Her own 800 for the investigation remains separate. Later projects at Wilde's have base costs of 1000 / 3000 / 5000 / 8000; the last three are half price at the required reputation, without spending reputation. Native quotes apply. No deadline or interest. Unfinished projects do not cancel the rescue or a confirmed romance.
I told you: the day this starts to feel like I'm being used to settle a debt, I leave.
You don't want to talk about the crate again. I can't pretend it never happened. This ends here.
You handed over Mother's research disk?
...Yes.
Where's Mother? Did you see the release papers?
You have no verified news to offer.
I didn't ask how much you got. I asked where she is.
On the first day I told you. Mother and the research were outside the agreement.
I did the agreed work, told you everything I knew, waited while you checked the news. Why doesn't your promise to tell me first count?
Eleanor—
Don't call me back here. I'm done working in this place.
I heard it from someone else. You've already published the research.
Yes.
My mother has no protection yet. You knew. So did I.
So I'm meant to tell you everything, but you don't have to say a word.
The agreement is over. What I do from now on is no longer yours to be told.
Then let's make a new agreement. No end date this time.
I hear you. Come here, my lady.
Since it's your choice, I'll take that 'master' to heart.
Respond to her choice to stay and continue your relationship.
This time she brings no accounts, and no goods for you to inspect.
Today it's my turn to pick you up.
Dressed for the Upper Level, she stands in the doorway and waits for you to speak.
...Who are you wearing that for?
Look first. Ask when you've had enough.
...Fine. I'll give you another moment.
What's the occasion tonight?
There's a party upstairs. The invitation has a space for a companion's name.
A difficult space to fill?
Too many people want their name there. Flowers, reserved seats, and reminders that a 'suitable companion' would be good for business.
Including that table you turned down last time?
That one too.
She lays the invitation on the counter and slides it towards you. The companion's space is blank.
I've told them about you. But some still think I'm only being polite to the shopkeeper who put up the money.
So tonight you intend to make it clear.
I also want a dance with you. Don't only hear the first part.
And these clothes?
A clean coat will do. I'm bringing you, not your clothes.
Good. I'll wait here.
And the blank space?
Fill it in yourself.
You write your name. She glances at it, closes the invitation and holds out her hand.
Come on. Tonight no one's asking you to inspect their stock.
...I did spring this on you.
I'm not refusing to come. Next time, I'll clear the time in advance.
Remember, that was your promise.
She puts away the invitation, then glances back from the doorway.
You can tell me whether you like the dress now, though.
Very much.
Mm. I'll wear it for you next time.
That evening, she holds your arm all the way from the shop. In the entrance hall, someone greets her by name, then pauses at the sight of you.
And this is—
My partner.
She doesn't wait for a guess.
He runs a pawnshop in the Lower Levels. The one I keep telling you about.
I see... Please, come in.
Some take another look at you; others raise a glass. She returns each greeting without letting go. She leaves the reserved seat empty and takes you to the other side.
You answered quickly.
Nothing to think about.
A man you've never met, but whom she plainly knows, approaches with a glass. The manager from that large purchasing firm.
Miss Eleanor. ...The proprietor of that pawnshop on your list?
Yes. The one whose name I didn't remove a single letter from.
A pleasure. About next season's supply, perhaps we could—
Discuss the goods with her. My shop is only one end of the route she's built.
...Understood. I'll pay a visit another day.
As he leaves, she lowers her head for a sip of wine, unable to hide her smile.
The same answer you gave that buyer last time.
Same answer. Different audience.
...Why haven't you asked why I'm not calling you Master tonight?
A private name. Your rule. I remember.
She leans closer, her voice for you alone.
...When we get back.
The music changes by the dance floor. She offers you her hand.
Dancing is your territory. Tonight I'll follow.
For now. When you learn, you can lead.
Your first step is awkward. She doesn't laugh. The voices recede behind the music, her hand resting on your shoulder, her eyes staying on you.
This is good.
As the party ends, she answers a business enquiry, then slips her hand back through your arm for the walk down together.
Was leaving that seat empty worth it?
Yes. Next time someone asks, they'll know who I mean.
The lights and music fade behind you. You return to familiar streets. Life at the pawnshop carries on.
I went to that party on my own. Left the companion's space blank.
Did anyone ask?
They did. I said he couldn't leave the shop. ...Next time you're stuck there, I'll come and carry you out myself.
We're in the paper. 'Mysterious companion'—I told them exactly what you do.
They probably haven't visited my shop.
Then let them come. Quote your usual prices.
You too?
Business as usual. The rest can wait until the customers leave.
The next party has a date. You said you'd clear the time—how about tomorrow evening?
Kept the time free today? I've brought the invitation. You still have to write your own name.
We missed that party. This is another one; I've brought the invitation. Can you come with me this time?
Then I'll go on my own. Get your work done, but don't forget to eat.
I've decided. Give him the drive and take the three hundred.
He wants the drive, not to help with the rescue. Taking these three hundred credits means abandoning your promise to her.
Someone at the commissary asked me to bring this for an estimate. Don't buy it; they want it valued. I've written down my reasoning too. I want to hear where we differ.
Want to compare notes?
If I only remember your number, I still won't know next time.
Then look at the thing properly before talking price.
I saw how clean it was and wanted to add something for that. I hadn't written down what justified it.
Clean is presentation. Record what it's worth separately from the work you put into it.
...Understood. I'll write down the reasoning, not just copy your number.
Let's leave it for today. I'll write my reasoning clearly and check it next time.
If you're unsure, don't rush to price the whole lot.
Mm. That part sank in.
Remember the screwdriver we valued for the commissary? This time I priced the goods first and recorded cleaning and transport separately.
No longer starting with how pretty it looks?
I still look. I just don't let that set the price for me. I haven't forgotten what you said.
This time I wrote down where every figure came from. I marked what I wasn't sure of, instead of agreeing a price for the entire lot.
Then you can discuss it item by item.
Mm. Even if we disagree, I'll know where the difference is.
Remember the people renovating their growing room, our first order? They asked again.
How did the last lot work out?
It passed inspection. Not one return. This time they asked when they could see the next lot, and specifically whether I'd still be handling it.
What did you tell them?
I asked what they needed and when. I haven't promised to conjure it up every time.
Then wait for the list.
Mm. ...People used to approach me mostly to ask my mother something. This time, they asked for me first.
You earned that.
I know. That's why I wanted to tell you first.
As the shutter rises, you see her waiting outside. She steps towards the sound, still gripping her bag strap.
This early?
My mother is out. I've seen her. I got her settled, then came straight here.
I meant to wait until you opened... Still came too early.
Come in. Start at the beginning.
As the shutter rises, you see her waiting outside. She steps towards the sound, still gripping her bag strap.
This early?
My mother has been moved to safety. I've just come from seeing her.
I meant to wait until you opened... Still came too early.
Come in. Start at the beginning.
Today I'm only selling. Usual prices. Nothing else.
Put them out.
Fine.
Then don't take them. It's not as if this is the only shop I can go to.
*She puts the goods away, her hand resting on the bag strap, and does not leave at once*
The detective's started on Mother's case. He says what he finds may be bigger than I expect.
How big?
Big enough that knowing the truth won't be enough.
Even if we find out who did this to her — getting her out takes connections. Getting back upstairs takes capital. I have neither.
...Don't answer that. I didn't come here to tell you any of this.
I take back what I said that day. Once we know the truth, I'll help you.
You said I'd have to obey you. And not just in business. I heard you.
You did. I was wrong to say it.
And putting it nicely makes those terms disappear?
Those terms are gone. You can turn down today's offer and keep investigating.
She watches you, then sets her bag down again. Her hand stays on the strap.
I can't repay a loan. I won't take charity.
Then work here. Inspect goods, keep accounts, run errands. I'll help with what you can't manage alone.
And you can manage it?
We'll find out one thing at a time. I'll tell you when I can't.
...Tell me about the work first. Don't think I've forgotten what you said.
Then we'll try it this way. I'll do the work. I'll also watch what happens to your promises.
Good.
Don't start ordering me about already. I haven't seen you deliver yet.
Bring the detective's findings here first.
...That I can do. I need somewhere to lay out what he tells me anyway.
She shoulders her bag. She doesn't turn at the doorway this time. A few steps outside, she slows.
...You'd better not be doing this just to see whether I'd agree.
No. I was thinking too far ahead again.
That actually sounded human this time.
If the investigator finds anything, I'll still come.
I was wrong that day. Arrange the investigation yourself. Come to me if you need anything.
...At least you know how to apologize first.
Fine. That's the end of it. From now on, say what you mean. Don't make me guess what 'listen to me' was supposed to include.
We'll talk things through.
Mm. If the investigator finds anything, I'll come.
Let's leave it. Follow your own investigation plan.
No charge. Return to the original relationship.
Then it's settled.
No charge. The old 800 is recorded as waived, and the agreement is made.
I take back what I said that day. Let me put it another way: once the truth is clear, I'll help you.
No charge. After the terms, you may still return to the ordinary relationship at the final confirmation.
I was wrong that day. Arrange the investigation yourself. Come to me if you need anything.
No charge. The original relationship continues, and the drive and later events proceed as before.
There. Eight hundred for the detective to investigate Mother's case. All of it.
Count it again.
I've counted it three times! Eight hundred. Every last credit.
That used to be just a line on a bill. Now, point to any part of it and I can tell you how I earned it.
Including that lump you insisted wasn't scrap?
The materials inside it sold. You don't have to like it, but show some respect for its contribution.
I've got the money for the detective to investigate Mother's case. Another shop took the rest, and the odd-job people agreed to an advance.
What about the next few days?
I'll keep working. Advancing the pay doesn't make the work do itself.
I sold the locket too. Stop staring at my neckline. I'm still getting used to it myself.
Do you know who bought it?
Yes. Mother comes first. Don't let me being sentimental hold everything else up.
The investigator starts tomorrow. He agreed to check the work records first, rather than question people at the company.
And after he finds out?
...After what?
After he finds out who did this to her. What then?
Then we... take it to court.
Will the court look at it?
*Her fingers go still on the stack of money.*
I don't know. I can't even get into the Upper Level. I can't afford a lawyer, and I don't know anyone who still answers my calls.
All I know is that we investigate first. Once we know the truth, there has to be a next step.
I can help with what comes next.
Help? A loan, or charity?
You could work here. Inspect goods, keep accounts, run errands. I'll help work out what to do about the case.
...Do you need someone, or are you inventing a reason for me to take your money?
There's work. And I'll still tell you if it isn't done properly.
I can clean a counter. I'm learning the goods. How far can your help actually go?
We'll need to check the paperwork and find the right people. I've dealt with that in business. I won't promise what I can't secure.
I don't want to hear that something will turn up. I can say that myself.
Then one thing at a time. Judge the results.
She looks down at the money she earned, pressing her thumb over the crease in the top note.
I'll hear the terms. Don't change your manner if I turn them down.
You can keep bringing goods as usual.
First, the term. You help me return to the Upper Level; I work here. Under my own name, not in a seat someone keeps empty for me.
A pass won't finish it.
Right. They must want me there because I'm good at the work. Not because of whose daughter I am.
And my investigation, other jobs and mother's affairs keep their time. I'll tell you if something comes up. I can't drop everything when you call.
We'll arrange the shop work ahead.
Mother and the research aren't part of this agreement. Who gets the drive and what course we take must be discussed separately.
You'll know every step.
Discussed together. Telling me isn't the same as deciding for me.
Together.
...And put away that tone. The one that expects to be called master.
See what I do first.
I will. If I think you're making me pay with myself, I'll leave. We can agree on work. Don't start adding anything else.
I have a term too. *You set another stack beside hers.* Eight hundred. Wages in advance.
I said I don't want a handout—
It isn't a handout. It's pay. Your mother will need medicine and somewhere to live when she's out. A payment before you start. Shop policy.
Whose policy?
Mine.
...You certainly know how to word things.
I'm paying the investigator myself. I earned that money. Nobody takes that away from me.
It's yours to begin with.
She separates the two piles. The detective's goes into an old envelope. She picks up your money, then puts it back on the counter.
Set my work days first. If there's news about mother, I have to go.
See the detective tomorrow. Bring the news back, then we'll arrange it.
This money...is for her medicine and somewhere to live. Not because I failed to raise the investigation fee.
Two accounts. Keep them separate.
Only then does she put your money away separately. Her fingers pause on the clasp.
I won't shirk the work. Don't let your side stay a promise.
Understood.
...Tomorrow, then.
Let's leave it. Follow your own plan for the investigation.
...You'd better not be testing whether I'd take the money.
I got ahead of myself.
Not that far ahead. You just have an infuriating way of saying things.
If there's news tomorrow, I'll still come by.
The detective found something. I read it all night. There are still things I can't make out.
Check the doorway first.
I took a detour and changed the meeting place. You're not the only one who knows to be careful.
Sit down. Lay out what you're unsure about.
The drive was hidden in Mother's old laboratory. The investigator couldn't open it. There's a password.
Do you know it?
My birthday. She always said that way she wouldn't forget. I've told her so many times not to use it as a password.
...It's genetic research on Nutrifruit.
She found a way to make ordinary Nutrifruit produce seeds again. Plant it, harvest it, and keep seeds for the next crop.
So people wouldn't have to buy from Pastel every time.
There are records ordering her to stop the trials. Then her access was revoked. And then... the charge.
She never embezzled anything. She just touched the business they least wanted anyone touching.
This gives us a motive. Getting them to release her will take something else.
I know. But for once, I have more than 'my mother wouldn't do that.'
Before the drive, there's something else. When that man pretending to be your uncle brought the box, I saw something was wrong. I didn't warn you.
Her hand stops at her bag. She pushes the half-withdrawn papers back inside.
...You're telling me now?
Yes. I should have told you then.
I kept wondering whether I couldn't see anything for myself. You were here watching.
I'm sorry.
And after one apology, I'm supposed to take out the drive and follow your arrangements?
No. You can take it away.
...From now on, tell me first. Danger, unpleasant news, all of it. Don't choose what I get to hear.
I'll keep the drive. We can discuss what comes next. The shop agreement ends here.
You don't owe me anything.
Remember that. Let it show in what you say from now on.
Leave the drive here for now. I can watch the counter. Safer than carrying it from job to job.
Keeping it is one thing. I decide who gets it.
Put it on this receipt. Take it back whenever you come for it.
She reads the receipt, looks at your hand resting on the counter, then slowly lets go of the drive.
I'll come and check.
Do.
Keep it on you. If someone asks here, I'll deal with them first.
You're putting your shop in front of it?
They know you come here. Another shop won't erase that.
Tell me as soon as anyone comes. Don't make a deal and then expect me to follow it.
Including what they offer.
...All right. I'll keep the drive.
Also, you've mixed several little components together. One of the labels has fallen off.
Can you tell them apart?
You spent so long picking through my goods last time. I wasn't only standing there being angry.
Separate them, then. Anything you're unsure about, leave for me.
She sorts the small parts, hesitates over one, then places it in front of you.
This casing was replaced. The price on the label hasn't changed.
Check inside too. A replaced casing doesn't mean it's broken.
I didn't say it was broken.
Then don't put it with the broken ones yet.
She looks at the pile, takes the part back and places it under the light again.
...Explain how to check. I'll do it myself next time.
Boss, you've been getting close to Eleanor lately. The girl from the Upper Level.
Someone got you out?
Then you should understand I'm not here on my own account.
Say it.
She's got a data drive. Hand it over first. Someone will tell her where to collect her mother, alive in the Lower Level.
Deliver first, then wait for your address?
Who else will you check with? Keep delaying and her mother might not last.
Who arranges the release, and when do we see her? Come back with that in writing.
Three hundred if it works. You're a shopkeeper. Don't shut out your own payment.
Write that down too. She needs to know what you're paying me to do.
They say she works for you now. Your word carries more weight than ours.
I haven't agreed for her.
Then pass it on quickly. Her mother can't wait.
*He glances behind the counter* It's not here?
I've got everything here. Just not what you're looking for.
Her name and yours will both be on the record. Think about that.
So will the message you brought.
Don't keep her waiting. Her mother doesn't have the time.
What do we start with today? Those things you mentioned—
Sit down first. Someone from the black market came by. About your mother and that research disk.
You write down the man's words in order for her, including the three hundred credits.
The drive first, then they tell me where to collect her. ...At least they're willing to talk.
Do you know whether this man can arrange her release?
I can ask. If I can meet someone who'll act—
With the drive, or with this paper?
...Do you think I stop listening the moment I'm frightened?
I'm worried that once you're there, only they can change the meeting. They take the drive, and you're still waiting for their next word.
She folds away the line saying drive first, then opens it again. Her fingertip stays on it.
What can I do now? Will sitting here get mother out?
Check where she's held, who handles the paperwork and where she can be seen. Leave the original here. Every question you ask still leaves you a way back.
I have her medication records. The person collecting it signed. I know the name.
Start with that name.
...I'll do that. If all I get is wait again, we'll need another way.
There are channels for a protected transfer. We submit material they can act on, confirm who takes responsibility, then discuss publication.
I'll find her medication records. I have her identification too. I know what can't be left out.
I don't have connections that can guarantee her safety. Negotiating an exchange is safer for now.
Then don't pretend it's arranged just to make me feel better. I'd rather hear the truth.
You promised me an Upper Level. Right now I just want to see her.
This comes first. I'll tell you exactly how far we get.
...Don't just tell me not to worry. I'm afraid I really will sit and wait on those words.
When we have something, we lay it out here and check it.
All right. This time, we'll try your way.
Your mother first. We return the research, but verify the release papers and collection point before handing it over.
All right. I won't gamble with her life.
If she asks later, I'll explain. You don't have to carry this decision alone.
We apply for protection first. Once she's safe, we deal with the research. If protection falls through, we go back to the exchange.
Understood. We don't count unconfirmed things as done.
That's what you said about my goods: if you haven't checked it, don't add it to the price.
We could publish now. Without protection, they may kill her. I can't promise to save her.
Let me think. I can't take this road just because you say it exists.
I've decided. Send the research to the newspaper.
Are you sure you don't want to wait for protection?
Yes. Mother didn't do all this so it could stay locked on a drive forever.
But don't tell me she'll definitely be all right. I'll believe you.
I've decided. I'll leave the investigation, and our agreement ends here too.
The drive is yours. I can't promise anything about what comes next.
You promised me an Upper Level.
I know. That's why I'm saying it now, before I make a mess of it.
*She puts the drive away and says nothing for a long time*
...Good. At least you didn't pretend you could carry it.
I'll handle the rest myself.
Leave the shop work today. Write down what you need to ask, then rest.
I can't cancel tomorrow's job. I'll bring the papers, but later.
Later, then. This can wait.
...I thought you were going to tell me to follow your arrangements again.
You reserved that time.
I remember. Good that you do too.
I've brought the paperwork for getting Mother out. Checked every page. The dates match too.
Put them here. Have you eaten?
Yes. You?
In a minute.
That's what you said last time.
The name on the medication record checks out. But they changed the collection point.
Did you go?
Halfway. Then I came back. He said I wouldn't meet the next person without the drive.
She puts down the creased record. Its corner has gone soft under her fingers.
I nearly went. You can say you told me so.
You brought it back. We can still negotiate.
I found the original official. He'll let me check the release papers without going through that messenger.
Record the name, time and place separately. Once the official confirms, we arrange delivery.
...Go through it with me again. Especially the two steps he said we could skip.
I have the protection documents. They haven't confirmed who's taking over. I thought of sending the research first, to avoid another delay.
Once it's sent, who will wait for that confirmation on your behalf?
...Deliver first, then wait for someone else to speak. Again.
Medication on top. I'll check the channel; you check who's taking over. It isn't done until both match.
I copied the medicine she can't miss separately. If they can't answer that, a notice won't reassure me.
Ask exactly that.
We can't count the protection as arranged. We have no confirmed transfer for today.
The papers are ready, and it's still no?
Which is why we can't send the research first. We use the fallback: exchange it for her release, after checking the papers.
...I don't like this plan. But telling me now is better than leaving me waiting for something that hasn't happened.
She takes wrapped food from her bag and sets it beside the papers. She starts pushing it towards you, then stops.
Bought an extra portion. Pay for it normally. Don't say you'll add it to my wages.
How much?
...Never mind. Eat first. I need this space to finish sorting the papers.
After this page.
I'll wait. Don't miss anything.
She points out a date. Only after you've checked does she put a small tick beside it.
You already checked that one.
I know.
Still unsure?
...I need you to look before I count on the next step. Just today.
I saw mother. At the place we checked. The official hadn't changed either.
She's out?
Yes. I saw her first, checked her medicine and the papers, then handed over the drive.
The messenger tried to lead me somewhere else again. I didn't follow. In the end he had to step aside.
You held them to what you'd checked.
...If I'd gone straight there with the drive, I wouldn't even have known whom to ask where she was.
Now you do.
She asked how much weight I'd lost. I'd prepared so much to say. That one question undid all of it.
They sent the three hundred to the shop.
...Did you take it?
Returned it untouched. Told him to pass on a message: I don't do that kind of business here.
*She pauses* I thought you'd say to use it for my mother's medicine.
Medicine money has a proper source. That money had your mother's price written on it.
...You said that day I wasn't for sale.
Neither is she.
Mother's been transferred safely. I saw her. The person taking over went through every medicine with me.
No gap in her medicine?
None. When the application notice came first, I wanted to push you to send the research.
Then I checked and found they hadn't set the transfer time. If I'd sent it then...
You waited for confirmation.
Because you made me look at the notice again. ...I'll remember this time.
She complained my writing was too small. Nobody else would start with that.
Settle her first, then handle the research as agreed.
Yes. I remember the order.
I meant to come in, explain the paperwork properly, then discuss what comes next.
You still can.
...I can't get the words out.
Come here.
She comes around the counter and stops. You open your arms. At last she leans into you, forehead against your shoulder. She tries to speak, but her breathing breaks first.
...Let me stay a moment.
Stay.
All the way back, I kept thinking what to tell you first.
She's back.
...Yes. She's back.
Don't repeat what just happened to anyone.
Go be with her. There's no work for you here today.
Tomorrow, then?
Come if you want. Sort out those sleeves first. They nearly swept something off the counter last time.
...I know. I'll have the clothes altered myself. Don't order anything for me first.
I'll ask Wilde about a home. You and your mother need somewhere lasting.
She's out now. You're still taking care of the rest?
Getting her out wasn't all I promised.
...I'll go home first. We'll talk about tomorrow, tomorrow.
And the box. I haven't forgotten.
I know.
This time you told me who came, what they said, which steps hadn't worked.
More than once I wanted to blame you for delaying. Then I could only come back and ask you to check.
Next time too.
...Next time there's danger, tell me first. Don't wait for me to ask.
Hello. I've come for some household goods. Eleanor said not to choose the prettiest ones. Choose sturdy ones first.
She never used to shop like that.
Now she chooses for me, and complains that I'm too slow.
She didn't come with you?
She's running an errand. She explained the way here twice before leaving.
She said she earned the investigation money herself. What you gave her was wages in advance.
She said she earned the investigation money herself. Later she came back and discussed the terms of your help properly.
Yes. We agreed on terms.
She told me. Which days she comes, what you can't decide for her. She remembers clearly.
You're worried about her?
When she goes out now, she often says she'll ask the shopkeeper first. Then adds that something needs checking.
She asks carefully too.
I asked whether she was unsure of everything, or only felt safe after someone checked it with her.
What did she say?
Said I asked too many questions, and went out. Came back asking whether I'd need her for anything tomorrow.
Let her think about the rest herself. I've only just come back. I'm in no hurry to explain it for her.
It hurts to have given the research back. But she needn't explain herself every day for bringing me home.
She's afraid she disappointed you.
Then tell her this: the lamp still needs installing. We're both here. Let's start living the life in front of us.
I'll keep following up on the review and the research. You've both done a great deal of running around for me.
She made a list of things to do as well.
I saw it. Your shop takes up quite a few lines.
That's everything. Charge the usual price.
Her instructions?
She said not to mix household accounts with her wages.
Very clear accounts.
...She used to say she had everything worked out too. When it's time to decide, she still stands at the doorway a while.
I won't hurry her.
Good.
She's in her usual clothes, cuffs folded in and held with two stitches. As she enters, she looks first at the empty chair beside the counter.
The altered clothes aren't ready. This will do today. I won't sweep anything off again.
Sit. Look at this lot first.
...Mother doesn't need anything today. I finished everything there before coming.
I hadn't asked.
I'm telling you first. So you don't send me home again.
I've checked these. Written down prices too.
Let me see.
...The moment you hold out your hand, I want to turn the labels over again.
Afraid I'll find faults?
They looked right when I calculated them myself.
Then explain your calculations too.
My own goods first, then your work. Payment for goods and wages are separate.
Set them out.
I've put the damaged ones aside. Don't value them all together.
Saving me some trouble now?
I'm saving myself an argument over a fair price.
All right. About what I worked out.
If today isn't right, I'll ask elsewhere. I still agreed to do the work here, and I will.
I priced this too high. Saw the new casing, missed the wear inside.
Correct it. You caught something on the other one that I missed.
...Give me that one too.
The pen's beside you.
I know. I'll get it.
She picks up the pen, corrects her mistake first, then sets the two checked labels side by side.
Someone offered me a whole lot, cheaper. I was going to accept.
And now?
I'd like to bring it here and check it together. ...If you're busy, I'll come later.
Ask whether we can inspect the pieces separately. Bring your prices too.
All right.
She picks up her bag strap as though leaving immediately. After a moment, she sets it down again.
I've noticed I want to ask you first about everything now. That habit...I need to think about it.
And about the housing. Wilde's people came by.
The new place isn't big, but the light's good enough to read by, and Mother's things don't all have to be piled beside the bed. She asked me to tell you—
Don't empty the shop for us?
...How did you know?
A guess.
She also said you look better at keeping accounts than I did when I first came here. I'm repeating that exactly. I won't explain it.
I'll ask about that lot first. Bring the records next time.
Keep anything you're unsure about for us to look at.
...Don't make that sound so easy. I'm still trying to decide things for myself.
She wears the altered dark dress, white apron neatly fitted, headpiece carefully pinned. At the counter, her hands hesitate between her skirt and the tabletop.
Had the cuffs altered again. Tried inspecting and carrying things. They won't get in the way.
Did you ask about the lot?
We can inspect it separately. After I asked as you suggested, they withdrew two pieces and quoted again.
Check the rest just as carefully.
I know. Wrote my own prices. Didn't agree yet.
She puts the record beside your hand. This time she doesn't cover it with her own.
There's something we need to settle first. That crate from the man pretending to be my uncle. You already knew something was wrong with it.
I did. I should have told you.
I remember what you've done since. But don't use your help, or our agreement, to cover this up.
I won't. I was wrong. I'm sorry.
...Tell me things first from now on. Even the ugly ones. I don't want to be the last person to know.
She aligns the checked papers and sets down the pen, without reaching for her bag.
When you told me to hold on to the drive, I really thought of taking it myself.
You came back.
Yes. After mother got out, I thought I wouldn't need to come to you about everything.
But the lot, those two labels...my first thought is still to bring them for you to check.
You caught plenty yourself.
I know. I don't want you doing everything for me.
It's...after you've weighed it up, I can get on with my part. Without doing it and wondering what else I've missed.
She smooths a fold in her apron, then quickly takes her hand away.
When we made the agreement, I wouldn't stand for that ordering tone. You remember.
I remember.
I still won't accept everything.
I know.
But there are things I want your judgment on first. Not because I took those wages.
She starts as though to curtsy. Her fingers touch her skirt, then let go. After a moment, she looks up again.
...Master.
Before, I could say I used that name because it was in the agreement.
I have to own this part myself now. There are things I want your judgment on first.
I hear you.
Don't look as though you knew all along.
I hear you.
...Don't start teasing. I nearly changed it back just then.
Leave today's things here for now.
All right.
Her answer is quiet. Packing her bag, she glances back at the records, still unused to what she has just said.
Brought a business lead today.
Go on.
Someone wants usable old equipment and materials. I said they could look here. Didn't promise stock or a discount.
Have them come themselves.
Yes. ...I just wanted to tell you first.
That customer I sent to buy used equipment. Did he come by?
He did. Looked over the goods. We agreed on a price.
I'm asking about my judgment, not for a sales report!
If it didn't work out with that used-equipment buyer I sent, leave it. You don't have to sell to him just because I sent him.
Today's work is done.
You've been waiting for the right moment since you walked in. Say it. I'm listening.
...You noticed?
Same counter. You've wiped it three times.
Don't talk. Let me finish first, or I might not say it.
After mother got out, I found plenty of reasons. Work here, learn the goods, repay what you'd done little by little.
But even when I knew how to inspect something, I still wanted to show you. With nothing to ask, I'd wonder whether the shop was busy.
So that's why the counter needed cleaning three times?
Let me finish.
I thought about that name all the way here last time. Then all the way home after saying it.
I want to hear your judgment. I want to look after things here. But I want more than doing the work well.
She takes her hand off the cloth. At last she leaves every object on the counter alone.
I like you.
I want to be your lover. And stay here as the person you can call over, the one you can trust with things.
I've thought this through. You didn't decide it for me with that money.
I understand. Be my attendant, and my lover.
...You answered so quickly. I spent all night preparing, and I haven't finished.
Then save the rest. Tell me over time.
Come here.
What is it this time?
I want to hold your hand.
She gives you her hand. Only once she's holding yours does she slowly breathe out.
Then hold it properly. Don't let go at the first crooked item.
Any other terms?
That name stays private. I want that clear now.
Agreed.
And you still owe your half upstairs. Being my lover doesn't let you out of it.
It doesn't.
She loosens her hand, lifts her skirt a little, and this time slowly finishes the curtsy. Her face turns aside.
...Master. I'll follow your lead with today's work too.
I love you too. Let's end the agreement and just be lovers.
End it? ...And your half upstairs?
You can return under your own name. You don't need to exchange duties for it.
...You really do have faith in me.
All right. I'll call you by your name from now on. Don't pretend you didn't hear.
You're important to me. But I think we should stay friends.
...Understood.
Then the agreement ends here too. I don't want to be your attendant while pretending I never said any of this.
About the Upper Level—
I'll get there myself. I know where to start now. Thank you for that.
I'll still come when I have goods. And still argue if the price is wrong.
I only meant to buy something.
And now?
Now I have a question first. Does Eleanor really call you that?
She told you?
A while ago I asked why she was in such a hurry. She said, "Master doesn't know I'm coming in late today."
Then she stopped short herself. And told me not to make a fuss.
Did you manage it?
No.
She used to complain if someone carried her shopping bags at the wrong angle. Now she tells me you forget to eat and leave your pen everywhere.
She's still complaining.
I can hear that. But now she actually does something about it.
I asked whether she'd still not paid off that money. She said it was wages, not a loan, and told me not to turn everything into a debt.
I asked whether she owed you something. She said no. She'd come back later and renegotiated every term herself.
I had that bracelet examined afterward. Your price really was fair.
She looked prouder hearing me admit that than she does when someone praises her.
People upstairs are already talking. Saying she's down here, working as a pawnbroker's maid.
What do you say?
That she's dating the owner too. Telling half a story and leaving half out just sounds spiteful.
How did they take it?
About like I did the first time. You may look a little pleased. Not that pleased.
But I'm serious. She wants to go back under her own name. When that day comes, someone will use this against her to her face.
She's ready.
...You sound more certain than she does.
That's everything. Don't quote me some incomprehensible price just because I know your attendant.
She gave instructions. Friends pay the usual price.
...She really does speak for you now.
Mother's found a little work. Growing things. Nothing large, but she's taking it very seriously.
Will you help her?
Sometimes. She says not to stand over her all day. I'll only start picking at everything she does.
There's news about the research on making Nutrifruit seed again. That doesn't mean everyone will be eating their own crop tomorrow. There are trials to run, and people willing to run them.
And your mother?
Busy with the review, and explaining things to the people who received the data. Now she complains there aren't enough hours in a day.
Lydia says she can find me a position upstairs. I asked what it was. She said, first there's a place, the details later.
You're not going to take it.
...How do you know?
You don't want a position. You want them to remember your name.
...Right. I want to go back, but not like that.
She means well, I know. But I don't want to sit in a position where I don't even know what I'm supposed to do, waiting every month for someone to pay me out of respect for her.
Someone offering an introduction isn't a bad thing.
I didn't refuse the introduction. If she finds people willing to look at samples, of course I'll go. But the next time, they have to come to me because the goods are good and the delivery is on time.
We agreed it would be under my own name.
Then we do it the way we agreed.
Mm. ...So you still owe me that half.
Did Lydia come asking about us last time?
Whether you really call me that.
I knew it. When it slipped out, she looked as if I'd lost the entire Upper Level to you.
How did you explain it?

Didn't mention how annoying I am?

And this. I've always worn it. I want you to have it.
Your mother's locket?
She knows. She said not to claim later that I hadn't thought it through.
Have you?
I have. She can say my name to me herself now. I want this to stay with someone else who waits for me to come back.
I'll keep it safe.
Don't mix it in with the goods for sale. This one has no price tag.
Keep wearing it. I'll remember what you meant.
All right. Then every time you see it, remember. Don't pretend I never offered.
I've thought about finding the locket again. I haven't yet.
No hurry.
Yes. I don't have to produce an object today just to make myself understood.
No news from the investigation today. Nobody sent me with terms either.
Then what brings you here?
Work it out yourself.
Seeing your master?
...See? You can work things out.
You still arrange so many things badly here.
Who said this place didn't count as a shop?
Me. How many times do you want me to admit it?
And now?
It still isn't pretty. Same lamp. Same corner of the counter that catches my sleeve.
Yet you keep coming?
Yes. My master is here. Should I wipe someone else's counter instead?
I saved this for you. Perfume. It refills itself. Don't smell it and immediately ask what it sells for.
You don't want to keep it?
When I want to smell it, I can come find you.
I'll keep an eye on the scavenging sites too. I know a few places with things left, and a few people whose word isn't worth much.
Save me some effort, then.
It's to save you wasted trips. Not to save you doing anything at all.
Almost forgot. *She lays a folded paper on the counter.* Mother's review documents have been formally submitted.
They gave you a receipt this time?
Yes. Investigation report, transfer records, acknowledgment of the research delivery. Nothing missing. I made them write the date in front of me, so next time they can't say they lost it.
Keep it safe.
Of course. Mother's innocence can't depend on somebody remembering a spoken promise.
Today's work is done. Come here.
When you say that now, I can't tell whether it's more work or something else.
Something else.
She comes beside the counter, and you take her hand. She looks up at you for a moment, then leans in first and brushes your lips with hers.
No instruction needed this time.
You learn quickly.
Don't use your inspection voice.
I love you.
...That one will do. I love you too, Master.
One more thing. If I don't say it today, I'll put it off again.
Go on.
I used to think that once I got back upstairs, I could pretend none of this had happened.
I still want to go back. But not to forget this place.
I want them to see it clearly. Down here, I learned to judge goods, keep accounts, earn my own meals. I want to walk back under this name, without hiding from anyone, or hiding you.
Then we start preparing. Wilde has a list.
You've already thought ahead again.
Someone has to remember my half of the promise.
...I'll do my part properly. Don't ruin the shop trying to hurry yours.
Afraid Master will go bankrupt?
Afraid you'll turn your promise to me into another bill you never read.
At the door she turns back.\n'Until that day comes, I'm still your attendant,' she says. 'So take good care of what you owe me.'
Don't look at me like that. I've just been upstairs with the pass Wilde arranged. I came straight down without changing.
It suits you.
Of course it does. It's made to Upper Level standards. The cuff buttons, the height of the collar. Nothing out of place.
I used to have a whole wardrobe of clothes like this. Now there's just this one. I'm careful even sitting down in it.
Did you get in?
Yes. Look at the goods first. I'll tell you about it in a moment.
The checkpoint officer spent ages going through my documents. Halfway through, he looked up. 'You're the daughter from the embezzlement case?'
What did you say?
I said my name was Eleanor. It was on the documents.
Then he asked, 'I hear you're working as a pawnbroker's maid down below?'
Someone beside him laughed. Someone who used to come to dinner at our house. I called him Uncle when I was little.
Do you know the funniest part? I wasn't frightened at all.
I stood there thinking about the way you inspect goods. However fine someone's words, you look at the goods. If there's nothing wrong with them, the words don't need an answer.
The contact you arranged submitted my documents the day before. He recorded the name of every person who handled each procedure.
The officer's face changed when he saw those names. He went through the remaining pages very quickly.
What did the contact say?
'Nobody downstairs wants to mishandle a favor for that pawnbroker.' ...How many favors do you owe down here, and how many are owed to you?
Every procedure was followed properly. Every page stamped. Every expense listed.
He went back and forth, couldn't find a single fault, and finally had to push my papers back.
You said good goods can stand by their price. Turns out documents can too.
He finally said, 'Welcome back, Miss Eleanor.'
Before I left, that inspector tried getting friendly. I told him I was in a hurry. Someone was waiting downstairs.
The look on his face was about the same as mine when I first saw your price tags.
That inspector. What's his name?
...Why do you want to know?
Write it down. I'm not buying anything from him.
You really hold a grudge.
I keep accounts.
*She can't help a laugh* ...Then keep it.
Is that road long?

People recognized me. First they asked about Mother, then what I do now. I said I work in the Lower Level. The owner knows goods, and his accounts are cleaner than theirs.
Mother still can't go back. I asked very carefully. Reviewing my pass doesn't revoke her exile.
She says it's enough for me to go and do what I need to. I shouldn't stop my own life waiting for hers.
Mother's case is still under review. When people ask, I only tell them what's confirmed. I haven't promised the rest in advance.

Keep it safe. One step at a time.
Your name is on the pass. The agreement—

Then we keep going.
Yes. ...So you still owe me.
Master, tell me. Do I look better in this, or the other outfit?
This one's for the people upstairs.
And the other?
For me.
...Correct answer.
Don't speak yet. Look at this.
She sets a small parcel on the counter and unwraps it. Inside is a cleaned screwdriver, its tip unchipped and its handle secured again. A densely written label lies beside it.
The sample for my first order. A household upstairs is renovating its growing room. They want reliable used equipment and materials.
New is expensive. They don't trust used. People upstairs think nine out of ten things from down here are stolen.
How do you make them trust it?
Origin, condition, repairs, replacements. Everything on the label. I recorded who found each piece and in which scavenging area.
Goods from below, inspection below, buyers above. You need to understand both ends to make it work.
Inspect it. Just as you used to inspect my goods.
You pick up the screwdriver and turn it over. Check the tip, the handle joint, every detail on her label. She waits across the counter without speaking.
You're looking for faults.

*She breathes in very slowly, then out again.*
I've waited a long time to hear that.
Feeling pleased with yourself?
Yes. You're not allowed to tease me.
Before delivery, someone told that household my goods were stolen stock from a pawnshop.
Who?
An Upper Level dealer that's been trading in used goods for years. My family used to buy from them.
The household asked me about it. I laid out the origin records for every piece, and went through them page by page.
Finally they asked the dealer: can you produce records like these for your own goods?
Could they?
No.
I signed the contract. My own name.
The person who introduced me came out of regard for you. He said, 'People upstairs have heard about that pawnbroker's eye too.'
Training, samples, trial work. You didn't cut corners on any of it. They picked through it all evening and couldn't find any shoddy work.
It's all ordinary equipment and existing seeds. Nothing from the research we returned. I did use everything Mother taught me about the basics.
The public research trials asked about procurement too. I inspect and supply goods. I won't write Mother's research down as mine.
The training money wasn't wasted.
It wasn't just the training.
The first time I brought scavenged goods, you made me name a price, then explained what I'd got wrong. What I'm doing now is what I learned that day.
So half this order is yours.
Half's too much.
I say half, I mean half. ...Is it that difficult to give me proper credit, Master?
You did very well.
...That's better.
This is the pawnshop? ...Smaller than I expected.
Buying or selling?

There's a new supplier upstairs. Eleanor. Clean goods, complete records, fair prices. Several of us have been asking where she gets her stock.
Every trail leads here.
And?

My goods sell at my prices. Her business isn't mine to sell.
Not even for double?
Not for ten times as much.

What if she won't lower her price?

What did she say?

She said, 'Go ahead. He won't go around me.'

And now?

Mother still can't go upstairs. The night before, she made me rehearse it in our room and found three weak points.
People asked about all three today.
Then someone came to see me. One of the biggest procurement firms upstairs. The person in charge came in person.
The contract was worth more than all my current orders together.
The condition?
You can guess.
Remove that pawnshop downstairs from the supplier and partner list. People upstairs don't like dealing with pawnshops. And there are unpleasant rumors.
...Just like Lydia at the beginning. Back then it was 'stop mentioning your mother's case.' Today it's 'stop mentioning that pawnshop.'
What did you say?
In front of everyone.
'Where my goods come from, who inspected them, who provided my first capital: not a single name comes off that list. If you object to a pawnshop, find someone else.'
And then?
The whole room went quiet.
Then someone at the back came forward and said they'd sign. A little later, a second person did too.
When that manager left, his face looked worse than mine after my first Nutrifruit.
Half the people came through your connections. Someone told me they were there to show support for that shopkeeper.
I told them I didn't need a cheering section. Since they'd come, they should look at the goods.
Someone asked whether the supply was reliable. I said half the scavengers and owners downstairs knew my mas... my business partner.
You didn't hear that. I corrected it.
I heard.
...Then pretend you didn't. Lydia was the only person there who laughed.
The venue, the samples, the arrangements. You spared none of it. Nobody could claim this presentation only succeeded through someone else's influence.
Lydia was there too. Afterward she came running over, but the first thing she said wasn't praise.

'They kept calling you by your name.'
Only then did I realize. Not once all day did anyone call me 'the daughter from that case.'
Then the agreement—

Today I need to go home and change first.

Go on.

Until the day you walk back into the Upper Level under your own name.
That day has come.

Yes.

I turned down a very good dinner invitation upstairs today. Someone wanted to discuss next season's orders.

I said I already had plans.

Before, I was always thinking about what I still owed. That's settled now, and I still want to wear it for you.
I can walk into any shop upstairs. Discuss business with anyone. Turn down any table.
I choose this one.
She comes to your side. This time she need not smooth the apron or pull back her hand as it reaches for her skirt.
Master.

When we're alone—

Master.

She leans into your arms, her skirt brushing the counter. She paid to have this outfit made from an old dress. The first time she wore it here, she hadn't known where to put her hands, hadn't finished the curtsy. Now she can afford far finer clothes, and still chooses this set to see you.

For other people.

You haven't moved upstairs. The pawnshop opens as usual. There is still a familiar place for her beside the counter.

She can walk through those doors that once shut against her on her own. And she knows whose presence she chooses to bow her head in, before looking up again and saying, 'Master.'
